facts: The paper is titled "Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks."
The authors are from institutions including the University of Oxford, EPFL, and Stanford University.
The paper emphasizes the importance of accurately measuring what large language models are intended to assess.
The authors argue for refining benchmarks to better capture the capabilities and limitations of large language models.
The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is essential for understanding their capabilities.
A systematic review analyzed 445 LLM benchmarks from natural language processing and machine learning conferences.
The review was conducted by a team of 29 expert reviewers.
The authors provided eight key recommendations for improving LLM benchmarks.

The development of large language models relies on benchmarks and evaluations. A systematic review of 445 articles from major ML and NLP conferences was conducted. Many benchmarks suffer from weaknesses in defining and operationalizing key concepts. Recommendations for improving benchmark practices and an operational checklist for establishing construct validity are proposed.
Construct validity assesses whether a test accurately measures the intended phenomenon.
Face validity refers to the test's apparent validity.
Construct validity is essential for evaluating abstract abilities in large language models.
The interpretation of evaluations related to construct validity is debated.

The study reviewed 46,114 articles from machine learning and natural language processing conferences. The initial set of articles was filtered down to 522 based on specific criteria. A manual review by 29 experts reduced the selection to 445 articles. An a priori codebook was developed to assess construct validity in the articles.
The dataset includes responses to 21 question items across 445 benchmark articles.
78.2% of the reviewed benchmarks provide definitions of phenomena.
81.3% of benchmarks used exact matching as the primary scoring metric.
53.4% of articles provided evidence for their benchmark's construct validity.
The text outlines five recommendations for improving LLM benchmarks.
The recommendations aim to enhance the construct validity of benchmarks.
Not all recommendations will be relevant to every benchmark.
Each recommendation includes a specific checklist for developing a new benchmark.
78.2% of reviewed benchmarks include definitions.
47.8% of benchmarks use a negative definition to establish boundaries.
61.2% of benchmarks measure sub-components separately.
Combining measures can be beneficial when no single measure suffices.
21.1% of benchmarks require specific output formats.
Complex instructions may disproportionately affect weaker models.
Strategies to mitigate confounding effects include establishing baselines for relevant subtasks.
Factor analysis techniques are being explored to identify latent capabilities.
Effective sampling strategies are essential for constructing a representative dataset for evaluating tasks.
Many benchmarks currently rely on convenience sampling, which can lead to non-representative results.
Authors are recommended to utilize random or stratified sampling methods to enhance construct validity.
Task items should be designed to address common weaknesses of large language models, such as sensitivity to prompt variations.
38.2% of reviewed benchmarks reuse data.
7.7% of cases involve the reuse of datasets.
Authors should document changes made when reusing datasets.
Reporting differences between original and new datasets is crucial for construct validity.
Tests for detecting data contamination in benchmarks are essential.
Maintaining a held-out set of task items is important for ongoing evaluation.
Contamination can arise from direct exposure to benchmark items or memorization.
Vetting test items for contamination is recommended during benchmark creation.
Statistical methods should be employed in benchmarking models.
Only 16.0% of reviewed benchmarks utilize statistical testing.
Demographics of human raters should be described in studies.
Metrics should reflect the variability of subjective labels.
The GSM8K benchmark is used as a practical example in the text.
A well-validated benchmark should correlate errors with the intended phenomenon.
The text recommends constructing a representative dataset to improve reliability.
The conclusion states that GSM8K is a valid benchmark for grade school math.

A systematic review of 445 benchmarks in NLP and ML literature identified significant gaps in construct validity. About half of the reviewed articles addressed validity, but most had weaknesses in at least one area. The review assessed 2,189 papers and achieved a precision of about 85%. The authors proposed eight recommendations and created a practical operational checklist to enhance construct validity.
